papers.title: Quantifying and Visualizing the Invisible Hazard of Infant Rebreathing
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rebreathing of expired gases during prone infant sleeping contributes to hypoxic and hypercapnic exposure, even without airway obstruction. We investigated how anatomical, physiological, and environmental factors influence aerodynamic rebreathing. METHODS: A dynamically scaled in vitro model simulated prone nasal breathing corresponding to infants weighing 2 to 5 kg, with nostril diameters of 3.2 to 6.0 mm and breathing frequencies of 25 to 40 breaths/min. Ambient temperature and sleep-surface characteristics were varied. Rebreathing was quantified using tracer measurements, while flow visualization revealed the underlying aerodynamic mechanisms. RESULTS: Rebreathing exceeded 60% despite unobstructed nasal openings. Increasing ambient temperature from 23 to 30 degrees C increased rebreathing by 68 to 77%, while reducing simulated infant mass from 5 to 2 kg increased rebreathing by 39 to 46%. Fibrous surfaces increased rebreathing, particularly near inclined nasal openings. A novel finding was that increasing nostril diameter from 3.2 to 6.0 mm increased rebreathing by up to 50%. Flow visualization revealed vortical structures that retained expired fluid near the nasal openings, facilitating re-inspiration. CONCLUSIONS: Aerodynamic rebreathing depends strongly on simulated infant characteristics and sleeping environments. These findings are consistent with established safe-sleep recommendations and identify nostril diameter, for the first time, as a potentially important anatomical factor warranting clinical investigation.

papers.title: A Common Recognition Architecture Across Memory Scales
papers.abstract: Recognition decisions occur across memory episodes that vary vastly in scale, from compact single-item episodes to extended experiences involving hundreds of items. To test how memory scale shapes the neural mechanisms underlying old/new judgments, we recorded EEG while participants performed a recognition memory task across set sizes ranging from 1 to 128 items (spanning 2 to 256 recognition judgments). Classic electrophysiological signatures of recognition, including frontal and parietal old/new effects, persisted continuously across set sizes. Furthermore, multivariate neural classifiers trained on small memory scales generalized robustly across set sizes. Rather than revealing distinct neural formats, increasing memory scale produced systematic, continuous shifts in the timing and strength of a shared recognition response: signals emerged progressively later and weaker at larger memory scales. Temporal-alignment and cross-correlation analyses demonstrated that responses across scales followed a common waveform trajectory, with timing shifts propagating into motor response preparation. Finally, individual difference analyses revealed that this common recognition format exhibits scale-dependent behavioral relevance, tracking working-memory capacity at smaller scales and long-term memory performance at larger scales. Together, these findings demonstrate that recognition signals share a common neural format across scale while changing dynamically in timing, strength, and behavioral relevance, providing evidence for convergence onto a shared recognition architecture.

papers.title: Pre-synaptic facilitation of corticospinal output improves dexterity and finemotor control after stroke
papers.abstract: The corticospinal tract (CST) is a neural pathway that supports skilled use of the arm and hand. Lesions of corticospinal axons result in muscle weakness, deficits of gross motor function, and loss of proximal and distal dexterous control for which effective treatments are still lacking. Here we exploited excitatory connections from motor thalamus to primary motor cortex to potentiate surviving descending signals and restore volitional arm and hand control in three monkeys with corticospinal tract lesion, using deep brain stimulation. Stimulation targeted to thalamocortical projections facilitated upper-limb movements, enabling monkeys with arm and hand paralysis to perform unconstrained 3D reach and fine dexterous tasks. Stimulation improved strength, hand gross motor function, and digits control. Electrophysiology suggested that effects were mediated by and more effective when targeting fibers with monosynaptic connection to the corticospinal motoneurons. Stimulation was delivered in continuous with FDA-clinically approved parameters holding realistic promises of clinical translation.

papers.title: Distinguishing evidence accumulation from choice confidence in neural signatures of perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: Human electrophysiology research has identified the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) as an apparent neural correlate of sensory evidence accumulation during perceptual decision-making. The CPP has also been shown to closely scale with subjective confidence. Coupled with the fact of its domain-generality and lack of choice selectivity, this observation raises the possibility that the CPP might in fact trace subjective confidence rather than cumulative evidence, two quantities that are closely correlated in most experiments. To disentangle confidence from cumulative evidence, we used predictive cues with 80% validity to manipulate prior expectations of participants during a contrast discrimination task while recording electroencephalography (EEG). At the time of decision termination, confidence is expected to reach a higher level for validly cued versus invalidly cued choices, whereas the opposite would be expected of a cumulative evidence signal due to biased decision starting points. As expected, valid cues led to faster, more accurate and more confident responses compared to invalid and neutral cues. At the neural level, cues produced systematic increases in preparation of the expected action prior to evidence onset as indexed by premotor mu/beta activity, consistent with cue-biased criterion adjustments. The pre-response CPP amplitude was significantly reduced for validly cued choices and the effect remained even when matching for confidence. Together these findings suggest that the CPP is not a direct read-out of subjective confidence, but an evidence accumulation signal that contributes to both decision formation and confidence estimation.

papers.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
papers.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.

papers.title: phyB photobodies display molecular memory, regulating light signaling transcriptional states through phase separation.
papers.abstract: Phytochrome B is a crucial red and far-red light sensor, which controls plant development and environmental responses to light and temperature. In the nucleus, phyB forms phase separated condensates, also called photobodies, consisting of various transcriptional regulators and transcription factors. phyB photobodies can form or disperse depending on the amount of light, the light quality, or ambient temperature. However, the biological relevance for forming photobodies is still unclear. In recent years the study of condensates has given rise to the idea that condensates can act as molecular memory, either due to long equilibration timescales arising from strong interactions that can kinetically trap a mixture in a phase-separated state beyond the equilibrium coexistence line, or from phase-separation dependent modification processes or transcriptional regulation. Here, we hypothesize that the formation of phyB photobodies and the associated sequestration of signaling molecules allows for the formation of cell-type specific memory about light conditions. To address this hypothesis, we first developed a live imaging setup of phyB photobodies which shows that they do not follow classic liquid-liquid phase separation dynamics, but instead have a restriction on their size, intensity and minimum number. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) then showed that photobodies between cell types have different levels of mobilities and diffusivities, suggesting that they are more stable in darkness or high red light, versus low red light. These differences in phyB photobody stability between cell types were also confirmed through whole-mount confocal imaging and single-nucleus transcriptomics in the same light-perturbation series. Through sci-Seq single nucleus spatial transcriptomics of the cotyledon in this light perturbation series, we identify a photobody-associated transcriptional cluster of nuclei that regulates photosynthesis, circadian rhythm, and RNA processing; the phyB photobody likely promotes its own stability by regulating TZP expression. The correlation between photobodies and transcriptional regulation shows how phyB condensates can provide cell-type specific light responses and exhibit signaling memory in changing environmental conditions.

papers.title: I err, therefore I am: Neural signature of error-monitoring predicts self-awareness in infants
papers.abstract: Self-reflection is central to human cognition and arguably a defining feature of human consciousness, yet the mechanisms enabling our mind to reflect upon itself and to construct a sense of self are unclear. Specifically, whether metacognition implies self-awareness, is independent of it, or emerges because of it, remains a subject of debate, fuelled by reports of metacognitive-like behaviour in preverbal infants and non-human animals. Building on evidence that 12-month-old infants show neural signatures of internal error-monitoring, we follow infants longitudinally from 12 to 18 months, when infants first start exhibiting evidence of a conceptual self-representation. Using a gaze-contingent match-to-sample paradigm with concurrent eye-tracking and EEG, we confirm that infants exhibit a neural signature of internal error-monitoring (error-related negativity, ERN) after making an incorrect decision (saccadic eye-movement) and before receiving visual feedback. Critically, we find that ERN at 12 months developmentally predicts which of the infants will evidence self-representation (mirror self-recognition) six months later. Infants' self-recognition was predicted specifically by internal error-monitoring, and not by external feedback-monitoring (FRN), nor by infants' age or general development. Moreover, we show that only infants who later self-recognised adjusted their behaviour post-error, by slowing their decisions and increasing visual exploration. Thus, internal error-detection, if available, can be utilised for online adjustments in information-seeking and decision-making as early as 12 months of age. These converging neural and behavioural findings support the idea that, rather than presupposing a self, early metacognition may be functionally involved in building conceptual self-awareness in humans.

papers.title: Divergence in sleep architecture associated with interspecific shifts in memory investment
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a critical role in stabilising memory. However, whether the architecture of sleep co-evolves with investment in learning and memory is unknown. To address this, we exploit the extreme levels of neural and behavioural divergence among Heliconiini butterflies. Compared to other Heliconiini, Heliconius have massively expanded mushroom bodies, the insect centres of learning and memory, which are associated with specific enhancements in visual learning and memory. Using a purpose-built video system, machine learning-facilitated behavioural tracking, and in-depth analysis of micro-behaviours during nighttime quiescence, we describe multi-state sleep in Heliconius melpomene and an outgroup Heliconiini, Dryas iulia. In both species, sleep is predominantly composed of quiet sleep, however, Heliconius and Dryas deviate in specific features. In Dryas iulia, quiet sleep is characterised by highly stereotyped, rhythmic antennal oscillations. Conversely, the antennae of Heliconius melpomene remain largely motionless but occasionally perform large movements which interrupt quiet sleep. These antennal deflections are associated with bouts of activity that include increased overall antennal displacement, isolated head twitching, proboscis movements and less frequently, wing movements. While these episodes were also seen in Dryas iulia, they were considerably less frequent. We further demonstrate that the behavioural profile of these active sleep bouts is constituently different from bouts of induced wakefulness, providing experimental support for multi-state sleep in Lepidoptera. This work shows that Heliconius melpomene, a species distinguished by its expanded mushroom bodies, exhibits more frequent bouts of active sleep than the outgroup species Dryas iulia. These findings raise the possibility that increased investment in learning and memory, as well as the structures that support it, may be associated with changes in sleep architecture.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression
papers.abstract: Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

papers.title: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks
papers.abstract: Decoding mental states from brain activity underpins brain-computer interfaces and cognitive neuroscience. Decoders are judged by how well they generalize to people left out of training, taken as evidence that they capture what transfers between brains. However, most benchmarks present the same experimental materials to every participant, so held-out participants are tested on materials the model has already seen. Here we show, across 15 EEG, fMRI and eye-tracking datasets and 318 matched comparisons, that shared materials inflate cross-participant accuracy by up to 46 percentage points. They also reorder methods, reversing the advantage of foundation models over handcrafted features on the largest emotion EEG benchmark. The inflation tracks cross-participant item identifiability and, in sealed prospective tests, vanished where items could not be identified. Adding training items improved new-material accuracy more reliably than adding participants. These findings call for reporting new-material accuracy alongside conventional scores and for measuring item identifiability first.

papers.title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
papers.abstract: Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

papers.title: Expression-System Biases Compromise the Functional Assessment of KCNH2 Variants and Clinical Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Background: Functional characterization of KCNH2 variants is essential for assessing pathogenicity in long QT syndrome type 2. Because hERG channels assemble as tetramers, the relative expression of wild-type (WT) and variant subunits critically influences channel function and pathogenicity assessment. However, commonly used experimental systems may not reproduce the balanced allelic expression observed in heterozygous patients. Methods: Allele-specific KCNH2 expression was analyzed in two independent RNA-sequencing datasets from human left ventricular tissue. Using the dominant-negative T74R hERG variant as a model, we calibrated the relationship between WT-to-variant expression ratios and hERG current amplitude. Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology, we compared 3 dual-expression strategies: internal ribosome entry site (IRES), P2A-linked tandem constructs, and dual cytomegalovirus promoter (dCMV) constructs. Co-electroporation of WT and variant plasmids in different ratios was the reference. Results: Allele-specific expression analysis supported balanced KCNH2 expression in human left ventricular tissue. At a 1:1 WT-to-T74R expression ratio, hERG current amplitude was reduced to 31.0% of WT, consistent with a dominant-negative mechanism in which incorporation of 2 or more T74R subunits renders the channel nonfunctional. All 3 dual-expression strategies produced substantial expression imbalances, with the first cassette consistently favored. IRES constructs showed the greatest asymmetry. P2A constructs partially improved expression balance but introduced an additional N-terminal proline in the second cassette altering T74R-associated trafficking and channel biophysics. The dCMV system also failed to achieve balanced expression, including after stable integration. Co-electroporation of separate WT and variant plasmids provided the most reliable means of controlling their relative expression. Conclusions: Commonly used dual-expression constructs do not reliably reproduce balanced WT and variant hERG expression, potentially distorting assessments of dominant-negative effects and variant pathogenicity. Co-electroporation of separate plasmids provides a robust approach for high-throughput functional phenotyping under heterozygous conditions, with implications for the interpretation of KCNH2 variants and potentially other genes encoding multimeric ion channels.

papers.title: Maternal separation remodels Purkinje cell circuits and impairs cerebellar synaptic plasticity
papers.abstract: Introduction: Early-life adversity has been associated with cerebellar abnormalities, but the cellular and circuit-level changes involved and their persistence across development remain poorly understood. We examined whether maternal separation (MS) disrupts cerebellar circuit maturation and whether these changes are accompanied by alterations in synaptic function and behavior. Methods: CD1 mice underwent daily maternal separation from postnatal day 2 to 18, whereas control litters remained undisturbed. Cerebellar alterations were assessed using transcriptomic and DNA methylation profiling, RT-qPCR, immunoblotting, Purkinje-cell morphometric analysis, and VGLUT1/VGLUT2 immunofluorescence. Patch-clamp electrophysiology was used to examine synaptic transmission and plasticity. Motor coordination, spontaneous locomotion, social approach, and stress-coping behavior were also evaluated. Results: RNA sequencing of whole cerebellar tissue revealed early transcriptional remodeling, involving synaptic transmission, neuronal architecture, and plasticity-related pathways. Consistent with this profile, we found that MS altered Purkinje cell dendritic arborization and excitatory input remodeling, together with deficits in cerebellar long-term synaptic plasticity and reduced BDNF-related signaling. In parallel, methylation analysis revealed hypermethylation of the glucocorticoid receptor promoter and reduced cerebellar receptor expression, indicating that early-life stress also engages stress-related epigenetic mechanisms in this region. Importantly, these neurobiological changes were associated with motor coordination deficits, altered stress-coping behavior, and impaired social interaction. Discussion: These findings identify the developing cerebellum as a target of early-life adversity and suggest that disrupted cerebellar maturation may contribute to lasting functional consequences. This study extends our understanding of the effects of maternal separation beyond the brain regions traditionally associated with stress responses.

papers.title: Open-BEATBox: an open-source autonomous operant chamber for high-throughput data acquisition of complex behaviour
papers.abstract: Behavioural neuroscience increasingly relies on rodent models to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying cognition in health and disease. However, conventional operant testing is typically restricted to short daily sessions that require frequent experimenter intervention and often rely on food or water restriction. These constraints limit behavioural sampling, disrupt natural activity patterns, and introduce variability associated with handling and experimental schedules.Here, we present the Open Platform for Experimental Neuroscience Behavioural and Autonomous Box (Open-BEATBox), an open-source, autonomous home-cage platform that enables continuous, self-paced assessment of complex cognitive behaviour in mice. By allowing animals to live in the testing environment throughout the experiment, Open-BEATBox supports longitudinal behavioural assessment across different cognitive tasks while minimizing experimenter intervention and preserving natural circadian activity. The platform is modular, customizable, and designed to accommodate a broad range of operant paradigms and integration with chronic neural recording and neuromodulation technologies.Using a visual reversal-learning task, we show that continuous autonomous testing generates approximately ten times more completed trials during reversal learning than conventional session-based protocols while reducing experimenter workload without evidence of major adverse effects on the welfare measures assessed. The flexibility of the platform further enables implementation of additional cognitive paradigms, including uncertainty-based decision-making tasks.Together, Open-BEATBox provides an accessible open platform for longitudinal cognitive phenotyping, facilitating the collection of large longitudinal behavioural datasets and creating new opportunities to combine continuous behavioural assessment with modern systems neuroscience approaches.

papers.title: Localization of candidate clock neurons in Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba)
papers.abstract: Organisms are exposed to predictable daily and seasonal environmental oscillations. Biological clocks enable organisms to anticipate these changes and coordinate physiology and behaviour accordingly. While circadian mechanisms are well studied in terrestrial model organisms, little is known about the neuronal organisation of biological clocks in non-model species, especially those inhabiting marine environments. Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is central to the functioning of the Southern Ocean ecosystem and relies on precise timing to cope with the extreme, high-latitude fluctuations in photoperiod, food availability, and sea-ice cover in its habitat. Despite evidence for circadian and seasonal rhythms in krill behaviour and physiology, the neuronal architecture underlying these timing processes has remained unresolved. In this study, we use in situ hybridisation and antibody staining to characterise the circadian clock in the krill brain. Immunostaining with an antibody against crustacean {beta}-pigment-dispersing hormone ({beta}-PDH) reveals distinct clusters of PDH-positive neurons in the eyestalks and dorsal central brain, along with an extensive PDH-positive fibre network. We further localise transcripts of the core clock genes cryptochrome-2 (cry2) and period (per) in cell clusters in the eyestalks, which also include the PDH-positive neurons. More specifically, PDH-positive neurons are a subgroup of the cry2- and per-positive cells. Together, these findings provide the first description of the neuronal architecture of the circadian clock in Antarctic krill and establish essential groundwork for future studies on biological timing and environmental adaptation.

papers.title: Macroscale dynamics of EEG microstates constitute the periodic and aperiodic features of the neural power spectrum
papers.abstract: The global signal characteristics of scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) are composed of periodic oscillatory rhythms and aperiodic broadband fluctuations that together comprise the neural power spectrum. Spectral decomposition of these features has long served as the primary window into the macroscale characteristics of human brain activity. Here, we propose that the primary periodic rhythms and majority share of broadband spectral power within the brain's dominant frequencies are the frequency-domain representations of the dynamics of EEG microstates. Microstates are characterized by a small repertoire of topographic voltage configurations that each reflect the momentary functional state of the cortex, and it is their time-domain dynamics that mathematically constitute periodic and aperiodic spectral features. We isolated and removed the spatial projections of distinct microstate configurations from high-density EEG using orthogonal subspace projection applied to both the surface scalp recordings and their modeled cortical generators to computationally test this dependency. Spectral parameterization of the residual power spectral density revealed that removing these spatial projections strongly attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and features of the aperiodic 1/f background. Selectively removing specific microstate configurations also demonstrated that each configuration aligned with spatially specific oscillatory and aperiodic 1/f components. Furthermore, correlational analyses of microstate temporal dynamics demonstrated that the average duration and temporal persistence of microstates strongly correlate with periodic alpha power, theta power, and the aperiodic 1/f background. Our findings suggest that dominant periodic and aperiodic spectral features are more accurately understood as the frequency-domain expressions of the dynamics of EEG microstates.
